items.title: The Health Effects of Eating Red Meat
items.summary:
The subtitle of the paper is Natural Experiment in Alpha-Gal Syndrome, and the authors are Vishal Patel , Christopher M. Worsham , Michael Liu-Hass & Anupam Jena .  The abstract:

Observational associations between red meat consumption and cardiometabolic disease are confounded by diet and other health behaviors. Alpha-gal syndrome, a tick-borne allergy to mammalian meat, leads to an abrupt and involuntary cessation of red meat consumption. Using national electronic health records, we compared changes in weight and cardiometabolic health over two years before and after newly detected alpha-gal syndrome with those in patients with other tick-borne diseases, who were also bitten and sought care but whose diagnoses carry no dietary restriction. Relative to this comparison group, diagnosis of alpha-gal syndrome led to a sustained 0.8 kg (95% CI, 0.6 to 1.0) reduction in body weight that increased with the degree of sensitization, as well as small reductions in triglycerides, glycated hemoglobin, glucose, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Not eating red meat appears to yield modest but measurable cardiometabolic benefits.

Those results will not make everyone happy.

The post The Health Effects of Eating Red Meat appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: The AI gains that gdp misses
items.summary:
That is a recent essay of mine , published in The Humanist Review of AI.  Excerpt:

One way to think of these matching gains is to say that AI helps consumers get hold of more customized products. The effective, available degree of product variety rises sharply due to AI. But again, that effect is not captured by typical, quality-based adjustments in how GDP is calculated.

Note that new, customized products typically involve higher gains in consumer welfare than older, established products. If there is a new product, or at least a product newly available to you (perhaps for informational reasons), ex ante the effective price of that product to you was infinity. You simply could not get it. But when that product becomes available, typically it does so at a pretty normal price. That is, in essence, a pretty large price decline, and if you value the new product a lot, as I did my Sokolov concert, the gains can be large. It is more difficult to reap comparably large gains by simply purchasing more of an established product that has been in front of you as a buying opportunity for a long period of time.

Here are other essays in the journal , including from Nobel Laureate Philippe Aghion.

items.title: The Tyranny of the Alphabet 2
items.summary:
I wrote about the Tyranny of the Alphabet many years ago. In economics the standard then was to list authors alphabetically:

Faculty members in top departments with surnames beginning with letters earlier in the alphabet are substantially more likely to be tenured, be fellows of the Econometric Society, and even win Nobel prizes (let’s see, Arrow, Buchanan, Coase…hmmm). No such effects are found in psychology where the alphabetical norm is not followed.

The tyranny is still with us. The AEA now lets coauthors certify a random order with the ⓡ symbol, as in Ray ⓡ Robson , but alphabetical order remains the norm.

Chris Dalla Riva has a nice example of alphabetical tyranny from the Grammys . From 2021 to 2025 the Grammys basically listed nominees alphabetically (the details are a bit messy see Dalla Riva for the full story), and lo and behold nominees with starting names beginning with A,B,C, D or E won suspiciously more than one would expect compared to the share of such names in the Billboard charts.

The post The Tyranny of the Alphabet 2 appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Increasing pay for lower wage workers
items.summary:
From 2014 to 2024, the share of U.S. hourly workers paid below $15 in real terms fell by two-thirds, from 38 percent to 13 percent. Why? We first distinguish the entry and exit of employers—wherein high-paying employers have supplanted low-paying ones—from organizational changes among incumbent employers. Organizational changes can be imposed on employers by external constraints, like labor market tightness, or emerge from the pursuit of new opportunities. Using panel data drawn from administrative records and job reviews, we bring this framework to bear on the recent wage gains at the bottom of the labor market. Contrary to predictions of creative destruction, we can trace only a small amount of these wage gains to the disappearance of low-wage organizations. Instead, the main driver of rising pay was low- and middle-paying incumbent employers of low-wage occupations increasing pay. These gains in low-wage occupations were associated with tightening labor markets and increased minimum wages. But over and above these external constraints, employers also pursued new opportunities for reorganizing work in low-skill jobs. Notwithstanding organizational inertia, major gains for workers’ pay can come from changes in existing workplaces.

That is from recent research by Clem Aeppli, Soohyun Roh, and Nathan Wilmers. Via the excellent Kevin Lewis .

items.title: Danish daughters
items.summary:
Using Danish administrative data, we compare parents of only children who experience a stroke at the same age and differ only in the gender of their child.

Before the stroke, parents of daughters and parents of sons follow similar health trajectories, with comparable levels of pre-existing conditions and healthcare utilization. After the stroke, a survival gap opens and grows, and parents of daughters are 1.5 percentage points more likely to be alive by year five. Over the same period, daughters adjust more than sons along several margins: they become more likely to live near their parents, less likely to be married, and have fewer children, consistent with greater involvement in informal caregiving.

Crucially, parents of daughters use more physical rehabilitation, an elective type of formal care that requires sustained engagement. Rather than crowding out formal provision, daughters appear more likely to help parents navigate and use professional services. Informal and formal care can therefore operate, at least in part, as complements in the response to severe health shocks.

That recent work is from recent work by Elin Colmsjö , Francesco Ruggieri, and Matteo Saccarola.  Via the excellent Samir Varma .

The post Danish daughters appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Will AI Growth Reach the Developing World?
items.summary:
Here is the abstract from a new NBER paper by Daniel Björkegren , David Lagakos & Mitchell VanVuren : 

This paper explores how economic growth driven by AI will impact the developing world. Our analysis is based on a growth model of a developed and developing economy where AI services are traded on the world market, and may substitute for or complement different labor inputs in production. Preferences allow for the possibility that demand for services provided by AI has an upper bound. The model predicts that developing countries may not benefit as much from AI-driven growth. First, they may lack complementary skills needed to fully utilize AI domestically. Second, they may be priced out of world markets due to their relatively lower productivity. We use our model to simulate how growth and welfare are affected by making workers more complementary to AI, subsidizing compute, speeding technology diffusion, and providing cash transfers. Numerical simulations of the model suggest that the potential for developing countries to be left behind – or having some workers lose in absolute terms – is substantial enough that researchers should study the impacts of AI on developing countries in real time.

I am more optimistic than the authors.  For one thing, in their model AI improves the productivity of legal services in say Africa, but not food.  That mix seems unlikely to me.  AI already makes rainfall prediction and crop management more productive, and it might over time help create more “miracle crops.”  A few other points:

items.title: A simple observation
items.summary:
The Riemann proof seems like a true surprise.  Yet on the same day Anthropic shares fell about ten percent.  In other words, the market feels that “capabilities” do not necessarily translate into significant social and economic outcomes.

Yet cybersecurity stocks are up considerably over the last few months, due to heightened cyber risk.  So the market is hardly unaware of AI and its potential, when the connection is real and evident.

Just a simple point to ponder.  Here are good comments from Alex Imas and Seb Krier .
